name: Vampire
baseMeaning: A pale figure with pointed fangs, dark hair, and a high black cape — draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood.
tldr: The vampire emoji 🧛 reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: a pale figure with pointed fangs, dark hair, and a high black cape. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood.

platformNotes.note: On Instagram 🧛 usually arrives as the tail of a caption rather than as a post of its own — a sign-off that reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood under a photo, or a reaction somebody left on a story.

In TikTok comments 🧛 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🧛 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for calling someone the office vampire, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🧛 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.
On X and Twitter 🧛 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like posting a late-night mood. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

generationalNotes.note: Gen X mostly uses 🧛 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🧛 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 🧛 to do the work of calling someone the office vampire, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood.
Millennials tend to send 🧛 deliberately, usually for something like posting a late-night mood, and they read draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood into it more often than the older cohorts do.

warnings.title: 🧛 and 🧟 get swapped
warnings.description: The Zombie 🧟 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the zombie is shambling and green, the vampire is composed and dressed for the night out. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🧛 as something else fairly often: it gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: What Does the Vampire Emoji 🧛 Mean? A Full Breakdown
seoDescription: The meaning of 🧛 Vampire in texts and DMs, with the vampire readings, the common misread, and the pickers it gets confused with.

longForm.overview:
This page is the untoned drawing. Somewhere below it are five versions of the same vampire with a skin tone applied, and those pages are about something different: not what the gesture means, but what a particular tone adds to it when it arrives from a particular face.

The short version. The vampire is for calling someone the office vampire and for posting a late-night mood, it gets misread often enough to be worth writing down, and it has five skin-tone versions worth reading on their own. The sections below take those in turn.

Unicode 10.0 is where 🧛 comes from. The drawing shows a pale figure with pointed fangs, dark hair, and a high black cape, it sits in the person-fantasy group of the set, and in a conversation it does one thing: it says what a sentence would have said less well.

What it says is draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — the picture does the same work as the words it replaces, and it gets there faster.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🧟 Zombie: the zombie is shambling and green, the vampire is composed and dressed for the night out. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
There is one habit that turns a small emoji into a misunderstanding. 🧛 goes back on its own, with no words around it, and it stands for whatever the sender had in mind — which was draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood. The reader gets the drawing and none of the context that produced it.

Start with Calling someone the office vampire. That is where the vampire earns its place: it closes a sentence that has already said the thing, and nobody has to add "you know what I mean". The other job is posting a late-night mood, and there the emoji is not the message but the temperature of the message.

The setting does half the work. 🧛 used for calling someone the office vampire in a work channel reads as a handover; the same move in a group chat reads as a joke. The emoji is not saying anything different — the audience is.

Which is also why this family has skin-tone pages. The gesture is the same in all five, and the tone you choose is the only part of the message that says anything about you.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
There is also a place where this emoji does not belong: the professional setting. 🧛 under a review, or in a first message to a client, reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and in that room the same reading sounds like somebody settling a point.

Two rules. First, 🧟 Zombie is a different message: the zombie is shambling and green, the vampire is composed and dressed for the night out. Do not send 🧛 when you meant that one. Second, a reaction to bad news needs words. A bare 🧛 reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and nobody in a thread about a person wants to be answered with a drawing of a gesture.

Not every message survives being turned into a picture. The emoji gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else, and the sentence underneath it loses the argument. Once 🧛 is carrying the meaning, the meaning has moved without either sender moving it.

With somebody you have just met, it is worse. 🧛 has no warmth in the drawing, and the gesture has picked up an edge of superiority from being used to answer other people.
longForm.howToReply:
If the intent is warmth, the sentence is the part that carries it. Sending 🧛 next to a message like calling someone the office vampire leaves the reader to guess whether it was draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood or something sharper.

If it was a reaction, 🧛 back is a complete answer. It says "same" without writing a word, and the exchange can end there.

If it was aimed at you, it needs text. 🧛 replying to 🧛 looks like a conversation between two drawings, and whatever the sender actually asked never gets answered.

When the register is unclear, the words win. The drawing gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else, so the sentence it was sent with is the only reliable guide to what it meant.

faqs.question: Is 🧛 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, but it gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🧛 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🧛 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under vampire show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🧛 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🧛 is used for draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood. The drawing shows a pale figure with pointed fangs, dark hair, and a high black cape, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🧛 and 🧟?
faqs.answer: The zombie is shambling and green, the vampire is composed and dressed for the night out. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🧛
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets usually taken as a Halloween joke when it is really about taking more than you give back, and about people who are up much later than everyone else more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.
The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.
A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as draining you dry, or a spooky costume mood, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.
